speaker: Speaker 1
words: I kept the seat for three years and we were successful in our teaching. We had to go back then for another year and then we got our life certificate. And then we could teach the rest of our life on our life certificate. And that was a two-year course. And that's what I taught on when I went back home about 15 years ago. And I taught for seven years of potlatch. I've been retired now seven years. And I still was teaching on the life certificate, although I went on to university and almost graduated. I took the correspondence courses and went to some schools. After I was 50, I did that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What courses did you take when you were at the normal school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I went to the rural, was in rural education because I was teaching in a rural school. And we took all the methods that you have to have, the methods of jurisdiction, language, and spelling. I almost flunked writing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Almost didn't get a T.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We called it penmanship. It was Palmer Method. I almost didn't get a T because of that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Almost didn't get a T.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I took it the last quarter. We were on quarters. And I almost failed it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Really? Really?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yes. If I had passed it, she actually would have gotten a T. And then I taught my three years. And then I went back for a year. And then I taught four more before I was married.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How many quarters did you need to take before you could go teach for the first time? Or could you just go teach for the first time?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, you had to go four quarters or a nine-month term. And we took our practice teaching in the country, six of us, and went out in the country to a country school. This was a two-room school out of Lewiston, Little East. And we lived in a little old house that didn't even have a bathroom in it. So the bathroom was out back. And we had a woman who was called a supervisor who lived with us. And the supervisor and me were the only teachers for these children. There were probably 25, 30 children in two rooms. Quite a few of them were Indian children. And we would take turns in the house. One week, two of us would buy the groceries, and two of us would cook the next week,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and two of us would do the cleaning.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That was part of our training, I think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You mean learning how to take care of yourself?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh, and help with the work. Of course, we had lots of fun. We had lots of arguments, too. Abusing ourselves.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you ever correspond with them, still?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't know where only two of them are. But the one, after I went to one quarter, and we didn't have to do that at the end of the first year. I went one quarter, and then I took my practice teaching. And then I met this girl from Moscow. And we went back and got an apartment and lived together. And then we both taught for years, and we went back and lived together the next three years. And we've been constant friends. She was in Forman, and we lived back and forth all the time. We've been friends for nearly 50 years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We still are a real good thing. Today we read in one of the stories that only single women were allowed to teach themselves.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It got to the place where there were too many teachers, and it was after the war, of course, after the big war. And they very seldom hired married girls. And I know of...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Why was that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, because there were too many teachers, and the single girl who did the work, the married woman, could keep house or home. They would hire the married men, but not the married women. And I have a little neighbor lady down below here that was married for about six months, but no one knew it. She didn't tell a school board or anybody. But she was married, so she would have lost her job.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did she get in trouble when they found out, too?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think they found out until the year was over. She was a good teacher, so they did not say too much. I think I'm going to be close to the bottom. One place I went to apply for school, it was just the one not too far from here, and my father and mother knew the family. And when I went to apply, he asked a lot of questions. And he says, do you dance? And before I could say anything, of course, I knew the dance, and I walked off.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I thought, I do that better than anything else.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Before I could answer, he says, well, I guess it's none of my business, because I know your dad, and he's a fine man. We'll take a chance on you.

speaker: Speaker 2

speaker: Speaker 1

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You weren't supposed to dance.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, he thought so, but I didn't stop dancing.

And Dad had gone out to the barn, and she had followed him along like little children do, and they'd gone up the hay mound. She'd gone up where he knew she had, and he came on down. She came behind him, and she hung herself on the scarf.

speaker: Speaker 2

speaker: Speaker 1

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Were you the middle? I was the middle. I had two older sisters and three younger brothers, and nobody had a happier childhood than I had. I just had the best time. I just can't remember any bad things, hardly, except that we didn't have a lot, but nobody else did, so we had a few clothes. I had lots of hand-me-downs. Everybody else had hand-me-downs, so we didn't mind.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You were in the car when you were growing up? Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The only thing that I remember that my heart was broken over was that I had two older sisters, so I would have to have the hand-me-downs, and usually I didn't mind because it would be something different. But my older sister had a coat, and it was the ugliest coat that was ever made. It was a tan coat with brown stripes and kind of coarse weave. She was through then, my second sister, me, and it was such good material, wool material, I had to have it, and I remember I cried when I had to wear that one. It was so ugly, and I don't think it ever wore out. I think I finally outgrew it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was always lucky. I was the oldest, but I always wore hand-me-up.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh, yeah. I always had hand-me-downs, but I can't remember minding too much, although I was happy when I got something new in my life.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did that happen very often?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think often enough that I didn't feel any privilege. I can't remember of it. And I was a tomboy, and I played a lot, and my mother being the nervous type, too, I was having a lost-child. But, see, I was the third one. We were two and a half years apart, or three, the girls, and then there was a six-year interval before my brother was born, and then 11 months and my next brother was born. So my job was to be with those boys on the farm and play with them. So, you see, by the time they were three or four ready to play, then I was eight or nine, and I spent several years just doing nothing but playing with them. I didn't have to work or anything, because I had two big sisters to work in the house, and my little boys were safe because I was with them. They weren't falling in the trees or getting hurt or something. I really just loved it. I thought that was great. We had lots of trees to climb and a big barn to play on and creeks to wade in and bird nests to hunt for. And really, I don't think that I have forgotten. I mean, a lot of people say you remember the good things, but it seems like my childhood was just extra happy. I had loving parents, and I can't remember that any of us were singled out as being better than the other ones.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you remember any birthdays or Christmases that were especially nice or memorable?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I remember about the best present I ever got for my birthday was a gold ring with my initial on it. They called them Cygnet rings, and that was quite something. I really thought that was great.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: When did you get that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: When I was 12. And then I remember going to high school, how frightened I was. We went to country school for eight years, and then we went to Palouse, which isn't a very big town, but I was really scared the first few days.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So I had a good life. Was that in ninth grade?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, and the reason I went to Palouse, we lived in Idaho, but I went to Palouse because the roads weren't paved in those days, and so they put the cars away in the wintertime, and you couldn't drive in them. And the railroad's right over here a little ways, and my dad would bring, my sister and I, it wasn't an apartment, it was just a room downtown, and my dad would bring us down to the railroad station down here. On Monday morning, and we'd get on the train and go to police. We'd stay in this room until Friday night, and then we'd come back Friday night, and he'd meet us down here. And we'd be in the machine on Friday night.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You boarded the train?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, we bagged. We ate apples and pancakes, candy bars and cheese.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How old were you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I was about 14.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Were you accepted in a high school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, because many of them were countries that went. And this particular lady had this house, this special for the, we couldn't have boys in our room or anything, and we all stayed at this one particular place. But we always went home on weekends. We loved our mother's cooking, and we were hardly awake. And the kids would say, well, I'm staying this weekend so we can do things, and we'd go around and have a lot of fun. And we just never did, but we usually drug someone home. We were great to have exes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But you were a good cook?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, wonderful. And she always said that on Sunday morning, both the boys, after we were all fairly grown up, and they had girlfriends and we had our boyfriends, she would say she didn't know how many to get breakfast for, because maybe the boys would have a girlfriend there, and maybe we'd have somebody, and so she never was sure how many.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Must have been really a warm and open person.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, everybody loved to come to her for meals. She was a plain good cook, you know, could cook vegetables and meats. She wasn't what you'd call the real thing. She cooked good bread.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did she cook for the hired help, too? Oh, yes. That's a really elaborate question.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I always think some of the funny things happened with the hired help. We had an old man who worked for us. Dad always had a hired man during the busy season, and he had a stiff finger. Something had happened to his finger, and I don't know, but anyway, you know how kids are today, oh, my mother would be so cross.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He would pass things around,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: that finger would stick out and the maids would look at me and I'd look at her and then of course then we'd start giggling. And then we had one hired man who always whipped the gravy. When the gravy went around, he'd take a spoon and whip the gravy and of course then maids and us would look at each other and there'd be another giggle spell, and once in a while we'd get sent away from the table.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you walk to the country school?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, but it was only half a mile. Some youngsters walked two miles, but we walked just half a mile. And I walked to the country school because I taught in it. Nobody ever took me. Usually it was about a mile, a mile and a half. We wouldn't call it a school no matter what the weather. If it was a big blizzard, we still walked.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: At that time, though, they didn't allow the school teachers to live next to the school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I wouldn't have anyway. I'd have been too weak of a coward. The last country school that I taught in, I boarded at a lady's home and there were so many children there. More children came there because the mother had passed away. I couldn't stand all day and all night, so I moved a little building in. My folks had a little building moved in and I had a practice touching their building. I could have had the schoolhouse.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It was real close.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I could have had it in the schoolyard, but I was too afraid. So I had it right next to theirs and I'd sit there. It was just about ten miles, but most days the roads were so bad you'd be shaking. And I'd ask. One room was where I was with a little woodshed on a Friday.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What influenced you to become a teacher?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think mainly after I got out of high school. I didn't study very hard in high school. I was really... I think I majored in a good time and my grades weren't very good. And so my folks were always willing to send us on school trips.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: They thought we would do what we should,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: but I just got by and that's all I cared. So there was nothing much to say about going on, so I worked in a boarding house in Potlatch. In those days there were lots of single men and they had boarding houses just for men. And I waited tables in the boarding house. And I had worked there about six months and I decided I didn't want to wait tables the rest of my life. But I had enough money that I could go one quarter and I knew that if I did all right this one quarter, then my folks would help me. And so I make my grades better than I'd ever done in high school, this first quarter. So then I got help from my folks. I've never been away from home very long. It's crazy to me at home, it was just in Liston, but it seems like it was a thousand miles away in those days. And I know that if my folks had sent me and said, you have to go to school, I would have quit and come home. But I was determined that I wouldn't after I'd made up my own mind. I'm sure I would have. And I was the one who did it in the beginning. I would have come home, I'm sure I would have. But after a little while I got over it. But at first I just thought I couldn't stand the homesickness.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Those old hills were just a barrier.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I still don't like those hills. They're kind of chaotic over there.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Liston seems huge and busy. Do you part from things?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, not so much. I worked for my board room the first quarter for a family. And helped with the housework and the cooking. Then it was the next quarter that I went out for a teacher's training and that was when I met this girl from law school and lived with her. No, I can't remember this.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If you look at families now, like your grandchildren and your son and his family, and you look at the family that you raised, and you look at your own family, you know, back when you were a child, do you think things are very different now? Or do you think that families and family life is pretty much the same?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, maybe it sounds like I'm bragging a little bit, but both of our families have their meals together. They don't grab them by the name of the community. That's taboo at both places. And I think that their family life are both real good. They have three children on the hill and two.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Our other boy has two.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they're real close. Both families are real close. And they go to many places and they go camping. They never go without their children except the one ten days they go every fall hunting, and that's the one time they have together that they don't have the children. I don't see as much difference as a lot of people do. I think it's supporting the families a lot, too. And I still think it's a lot the way children are raised. If they're raised as a family, they're going to have their families that way more or less, don't you think? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And I don't know. I just know from my own family. There were certain rules that we all had to eat together.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah. I know many families don't nowadays. They don't know how to eat. They just sit down at the table. And you're supposed to carry on as civil and someone who's active,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: concentration.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, and no quarreling at the table. No quarreling. Of course, giggling, we used to get sent away. Oh, yeah. Not that they're maybe perfect parents, but I really think they're doing real well with their families.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you're proud? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I really am. Of course, they have so much more than we had. But no one else had anything. We didn't have anything, but we didn't feel poor. If they had to live like maybe 50 the rest of the year

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and things like that, like we had to,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and handed down to the kids, it was terrible nowadays, but we didn't because everybody else did that way. A long underwear.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was your family self-sufficient?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you make on – did you grow on your own farm most of the real supplies? Oh, yes, yes. We always had several cows. We sold butter and made butter and sold butter. We had hundreds and hundreds of coats of clothing and raised our own needs and very self-sufficient. Usually in the fall, we would go to town to buy new underwear and socks and shoes and over shoes and things that we had. Maybe if we got a new coat, things we had to have, and I think sometimes that money came out of it, grain money. But usually all the groceries came from the cows and chickens and other sold goods.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How about you? Did you move to the farm where you couldn't have –

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, when we first moved here, we had chickens and – mostly for our own use, but we raised a big garden, but we buy probably as many groceries as anybody in town, you know, with exception, but having the garden. We lived just about the same as town people. Although our youngest son, he's a little bit like this. Maybe young people are kind of going back to the land he's putting in, or he's seen raising lots of garden. He wanted a goat, and his wife put her down on the mountain. And they are more that way than others. You don't know a lot of the things people are doing in the mountains.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You don't can a lot anymore?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Not since the children were raised, but I have done a great deal. I can do all I can to it until recently, and we don't use that much anymore. We use lots of fresh fruit like bananas and oranges and grapes. So I don't can as much, although I do can some every year, but fruit's getting high, and if I have to figure it, it doesn't pay.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You have to pay for the sugar. It's not even possible.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But both of our daughters and I, if there's some can, we make lots of jellies and jams, our own jellies and jams, pickles. We raise all our own potatoes, and we have black potatoes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was your father in wheat farming? Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He raised peas. They didn't raise peas yet. Peas came later after his time. But we raised peas and wheat and barley.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Where did you meet your husband? He was in Washington, D.C. You felt cold there? Yeah. He was in his fancy dress.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He lived about two miles down the road toward Perth. Oh, I used to see him to dances and things. Once in a while we'd dance together or something. But when we really started going to get a steady, we met down at the screen house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I see.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that was it. We went together seven years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Seven years?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isn't that terrible? The Depression came along, and in those days, women didn't support their husbands. That was, people just didn't want to do it that way. And Ernie was out of work, and he got enough money cutting wood to buy cigarettes and a little bit of gas. And he had a car, and he lived at home.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And you were working.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And I was working. But no woman wouldn't marry you unless you were married. And then, of course, if I, well, I couldn't have anyway, then I would have lost my job, too.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, because you couldn't be married.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And at the time, it was so hard at that time that I paid my, I paid the taxes for my dad for a few years, and I was making $100 a month. So I guess maybe I am a pioneer a little bit.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I think you are.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your father, did that bother him for you to pay? No, everybody was in, and he paid me back in later years when he had more money. Everybody was like, I said, being poor, we were all in the same boat. And a lot of them lost their farms because they couldn't pay their taxes. And because Dad was a good farmer, and then he had, they had their cows, and had this little cream check or butter check, they were able to weather the storm and get through without losing the farm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But it was tough.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just can't tell young people what a terrible depression is like. I hear people say, I'd like to see these young people nowadays go through a depression. I don't ever want anybody to go through a depression. Not like we did. I just wouldn't wish that on anybody.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How could people say that?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I just don't feel that way at all. It's a terrible thing. It just wasn't any money.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Of course, I didn't suffer because I was working,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and that was big money in those days. But it was really, really terrible. People committed suicide and lose their jobs.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you know people around here? Yes, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Even people we knew, they just couldn't take it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, I always think you guys get un-walled.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mm-hmm. Sometimes. No, sometimes. Locally.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. It was real rough. Do you think I could show you a couple of these two cars?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, not at all.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm falling asleep. I'm good. No. You're falling asleep. I'm just so tired. I'm having a long day.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was real hot out here, but you want me to warm up? No, that's fine. I'm just as warm as you are.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm yelling at her.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I've been called out before anyway. Oh, no, I just, um...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm going to go in the kitchen. I turned it off for a minute. How do you open this beside the check-in? You don't.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Okay. If you want beer, call. Is it still going?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, of course not. You said beer is on. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yeah, I had a big meal. And then this week, well, you can't see me over there. I'm afraid it's probably for anybody's good to be sick with the cough, there. The regrettable thing is that we didn't have a secret class. We don't have anybody working here. It's too early. It really was. I mean, you couldn't hear me all the time. Coffee won't keep you awake.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No. All of my sleep.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: My father-in-law drinks coffee like crazy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: It doesn't keep him awake.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can drink one cup a night. And that's, you know, I can drink coffee in the morning, but I drink too much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't think it makes anything. Not me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Something warm will even make me sleepy sometimes, even if it's coffee or tea. Oh, uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I like the milkman we went to. Full of sleep. I've been out and, you know, say, you know, drink a glass of milk and then I'm asleep.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did your parents, how did your parents feel about, you know, did they want you to marry him? Yes, they liked him very much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's so important.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He loved my mother. He liked my dad too, but the three sisters, all of the son-in-laws were so crazy about my mother and they all said they married the daughter because they couldn't raise a mother. And they loved to come to her meals. Both my older sister and myself never had a mother-in-law. Ernie lost his mother when he was 12 and Wai's husband lost his mother when he was about 10 years. So they, she was just kind of like a new mother to them. They hadn't had a mother for many years and she mothered them. Yes, he was real popular with the family.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How did you...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I was always...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think it's really sad some people do marry.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, you know, and I felt so sad about that one little story we had today and think how many times that happened in the time where they married just for convenience because this man was here and, you know, hardly working and not having any love. Wouldn't that be a terrible thing?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. I wouldn't want to live like that. Well, I think it happens more often than not.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think nowadays though we would get it at all if we just wouldn't do it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But you couldn't do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, no, it was way off in the post. Like my mother saw her mother only about four times after she came to the West. Even in those days you see.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Where was her mother? In Ireland. Oh, that's right. That's far.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: In those days it was. Nowadays you could get in a plane and go wherever you wanted to go. But there was no money. And it took so long. I didn't see my grandparents for many times.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Could you describe your courtship besides going to the grain stand with?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, we danced a lot, about twice a week.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What kind of dancing?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Was it like square dancing or didger-bogger? No, it was just what they called ballroom dancing.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Ballroom dancing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Walks and fox trots. And the chicken scratch and the turkey trot.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Could you do that for us, please? No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We didn't do too much square dancing. We did a little bit, not too much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Whose sponsor did that to you?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, there was a round hall over here about half a mile from our property. Just a couple men there in the hall and everybody went. And we danced with everybody. And we met all the kids from Garfield and Flushing and Moscow.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Even if you were engaged or married, you still danced with everybody?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, you always danced for stents, whoever you were engaged or married to. And the one before your lunch and then the last dance. And our song was what we called the Sweetheart from the time it was popular. That was our main song and it is today. So no matter if I had to dance with somebody else, I was just to dance. So we had that dance together. And that's our favorite song. And then there was another round hall over, I don't know if you remember. How long have you both been married?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I was just in Boston.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You remember the round hall that was over there. Well, I went to lots of dances there too. And then I went to, they had open-air pavilions in a lot of towns and we went to those. That was the main thing. Now these, like our little Randar, she's 15, she's great for dancing. You know, they used to have programs for high school. I don't know how old that was. And she says they danced with their date and that's all they ever danced with. I think that's too bad. But we met so many fun people from all over, you know, and we took some Spokane to look and did everything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, you know, dancing as an art, it was almost a sports dance. Yeah, that's what you did. Well, I think it was a requirement. And that was the reason. It required some skill.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I think that was special. That was what everyone did. And you didn't have to run to the taverns. There's nothing else to do but go to the taverns to the kids and all that. That's what they did. You have to have something to do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yeah, they don't learn dancing like you did. You know, real steps to make it interesting and exciting. Dances aren't really fun because you're only dancing with one person.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right over there to the clock there, Massey. A little mass colder? No, by the clock. By the clock.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: To the left of the clock? To the left of the clock.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, down below.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'm blind. I'm so blinded.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They always had something for everything in those days. They had spoon holders.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, you had a mat to hold it in? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I just grabbed one of the tables.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And now you've got one more. Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And if we went to a dance and we didn't dance to the dance,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: we felt like we were a wallflower.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We would usually have four or five dances ahead. And somebody asked you for a dance, you held up your hand, you had four, and you could just dance.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, really? Oh, yeah.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And it was real sad that you didn't get to dance to the dance.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, from your picture, you looked like you were pretty attractive.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I bet you got your ears filled up right away. Well, if you went all the time, you were all pretty. Yeah. And you could dance all the time.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was it according to whether you were pretty or not usually if your dance card was filled up?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I think it was more how well you danced. Mm-hmm. You know, if you were a good dancer. Yes, yes. And some of the boys you liked to dance with a lot better because they were a lot better dancers. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There's an article in the latest issue of Women's Sports about Baldwin dancing. And what do they say?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, they just say it's coming back,

speaker: Speaker 2
words: and it's really a tremendous feat. Not a great dance.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It seemed so funny to me at first to see him dancing. You couldn't tell his card was filled. Now it is, but I didn't really dance at all, no. In fact, I think we really danced cheek to cheek in those days, you know, real close.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My dad taught me to dance, and I loved following him. My father taught me. But I can never find a partner. I can't ever find anybody who really knows how to dance at my age.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You know, I had to look for an older man. No, you couldn't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So you'd have to be able to work well. Do you mind if I borrow Ernie some night? Yes, I mind. Oh, we'll let you come along.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He wasn't as crazy about dancing as I, but he would go with me all the time to see how much I loved to dance. But dancing wasn't quite as much fun for him as it was for me. But he didn't mind.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What other things did you like to do?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: On the porch, these would attack on, and you'd fall through the porch. And there was no sidewalk. It was so terribly run down. And we'd pump water out on the porch, and we had a little toilet in the back. And we had a new home in Moscow. We had built our own home in Moscow, but we were so determined to be farmers that we moved out to this anyway. But we soon had the bathroom in the start of the year, and we moved in.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: So the actual structure, though, is very old?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes. I told them we had good tuber floors and a pretty good foundation, and that's about all.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: The rest of it is. Looks like it had a couple fireplaces, didn't it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No. This was for the kitchen stove, and this was for the stove in the living room. We have electric heating and everything. We took out this pipe, this one, but there's one still up there that we don't use. But it didn't, oh, it was so much worse looking than that. I just got that a few days ago. My maid just gave it to me.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, what a nice present.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isn't that fun?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What a nice present. A nice present. Let's see. Was there a condition not to get married? I mean, were you seven years to get married?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, no, no, never. We were terribly in love.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Were you? Yes. Seven years is a long time. It's a terrible, long time to be in love.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, you had lots of good times.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did it meet your expectations? I mean, was marriage after you were married what you expected it to be?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yeah, yeah. I hadn't forgotten.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you have any suggestions for how to choose a maid that you're going to be happy with for all 40 or 50 years?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: For my granddaughter?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, for your granddaughter.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, you want to be in love. I know that. You know what that is. Terribly in love. I remember my girlfriend was married the same month I was, and she married a very fine man, and she says, I know we'll be a good husband, and we'll have a good life together, but she says, I'm not desperate in love with him. And I thought that was the funniest thing. I thought, goodness, how on earth did she feel that way?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did she grow to love him?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yes. They had a good life. And I think they loved each other, but I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But you prefer Bob for a good husband, a very old man.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He was a good provider. They had a happy time, I think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you discuss whether you would have children or not, and how many? Two.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We wanted two children. I never wanted to question that. I was 28 when we were married, and he was 27, so we were old enough that we didn't want to have children too long. Too many.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That's the Irish tradition, to marry later.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You want to get to 25, and then you can't have children. Well, I imagine if it hadn't been for depression, we would have been married much sooner, but that's really what. And we had seen how some of them had struggled so terribly after they'd married and just didn't even have enough to eat, and having babies, and how terrible hard it was to get along during the depression. It kind of taught us a little bit.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Was medical service really good during the depression? Were there doctors and things?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We had doctors, good doctors, but not... My folks never had any medical insurance that I remember of. But mine, you didn't have to pay as much. You'd go to the doctor for a dollar or two, and it was so much less. When our babies were born, it was $35 to the doctor. Let me see that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Thirty-five.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let me see when my mother had her babies. She had her babies at home, but mine were born in the hospital.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've always wondered about that. One thing I've never read in depression.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And my folks were always good to keep us. Sent us to the dentist. We always went to the dentist regularly. In fact, we have had a lot of work done on our kids, but there were five of us. And I'm in the middle, and none of us have dentures. And my mother lived through 91, and she had her own teeth.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, wow.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But we don't have such great teeth that we always went to a dentist. So pretty, but mine are colored to me. But some parents didn't do that. And the same with glasses. I wore glasses when I was in fourth grade, and that was quite amazing. I think I had exceptional parents. I don't know whether everybody thinks that about the parents or not. I do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I can remember. I mean, I've just got glasses since I was in fourth grade. I was just an agony.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Mine are little wires.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've had green things that looked like bat wings. It was all like this. I just hated it. Just hated it. I didn't think anybody wore glasses.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I thought it was terrible that you had to wear glasses.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had them when I was four. I was very, very afraid I had frowns on my face.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Our granddaughter wears frowns. It's long, beautiful.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've never been in a...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you tried?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I've tried.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I have too many waffles in my house. Our son's had two, and he said he had just tried so hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have a stomach. That's what she has, too.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It's quite a bit of work taking care of them. Otherwise, they're better, aren't they? Do you want some more coffee?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, this is enough. This is tough. What would you like your grandchildren to grow up to be?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Be happy. Be happy. I always said I didn't expect... These are my children, my grandchildren. They're doing great things, but if they could just be... Have a happy home life, that would be good.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you think life has been fulfilled for your children?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So far, but of course, you know, you see families look so happy and all of a sudden divorce. You don't know. I'm not going to say. It doesn't seem like it was possible. You don't think.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: If you say it, you know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I can't say. I hope it happens.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: This is sort of an interesting question, but... What... I see that you collect a lot of antiques. Is that what you mostly prefer to do during any leisure time that you have? Do you have some hobbies?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I don't care much about sewing. I've made quilts and braided rugs and recent furniture. That's collecting. That's what I mainly do.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you belong to any groups or anything? Any group that you...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The antique group. No, I don't.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How did you find out about our presentation today? What? How did you find out about our presentation today?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: It was announced in our church.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's right.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Let's see. I heard it in the paper, wasn't it? Just a little article about it. I saw it in there, too. But I didn't know what it was exactly.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You were just really excited that so many women came.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I was so sorry there weren't more. I could think of so many that would have enjoyed it that weren't there. I was wishing there would have been more.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think we'll be able to do a better job of publicity now that we've done it well.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And maybe explain a little more what it's about.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Because I heard several people say,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: well, I wonder what that is. And they were afraid, I think, that it would be something boring that they would have to sit all afternoon. And, you know, people have so many meetings anyway nowadays and belong to so many things that they get so involved that they don't like to do something they don't enjoy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you enjoy it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, yes. I really, really did.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But you wouldn't have taken a chance on it because you weren't sure what it was.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I really was. I do it. Another hobby, I do a terrible lot of reading. I always have at least two books going all the time. I get most of my books through the library at Lewiston. They come right in our mailbox and then I send them back.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, I didn't know you could do that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You can if you live in the country and don't have a library. Now, if you lived in Potlatch, you couldn't do that because of the library. But being in the country, you can do that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's a good thing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Right now I'm reading upstairs at the White House. Oh.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: J.B. West.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I heard it. Oh, that's just so fascinating. I like biographies and autobiographies. I think they're my favorite. That's why I enjoyed that today because that's really what they were. Yeah, yeah. And I know Elsie real well, Elsie Nelson. And her sister was my closest neighbor in Moscow. She's still a close friend.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's a good thing. I just flashed in your mind that I wanted to ask you. Oh, yes. In my family, my parents are pretty staunch Republicans, and I'm probably a flipped-away Democrat. How do you think your parents influenced you in terms of political views?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I have a real funny story about that. My mother was a strong Democrat, and my dad was a strong Republican. But they didn't quarrel a lot. They really had a custom. It wouldn't all be jokes, and so when it came time to vote, Dad would call my mother Mama a lot, and he'd say, well, I guess I'll go down and cancel Mama's vote. And she did. And they really were. And I'm not too. I think maybe I'll be more Democrat, but I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Probably this time.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I'll try to vote for the man, but maybe I'll be a little bit more of a Democrat.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What are your feelings about Roosevelt and getting out of the Depression?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you... Oh, I think he was great. And he was present for many years, and I thought it was quite an interesting period. I thought he did a lot.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you remember what you were doing when the Second World War started?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, that was when Pearl Harbor was... Oh, yes. I'll never forget. You know, isn't it funny how people say you quite often remember certain things? I was in the basement. It was on a Sunday, of course, and Ernie worked on Sundays when he worked at the premiere. We were in Moscow, and I was washing clothes. And Gary was tiny, and I was always so afraid something happened and that I'd run up and down the stairs about a dozen times while I was washing to see that he was okay. And I heard the flash on the radio. And I remember thinking the minute I heard it, I thought, oh, Ralph will go. It was a man that worked for them, and he was the only unmarried young man who worked at the premiere. And I thought that he'd be the first one to go. And sure enough, he was shot. He lived to come home, but he was struggling about it. Oh, I can just remember, and I can remember too exactly what I was doing when Kennedy was... I was teaching, and I came up the hallway, and one teacher stuck her head out the door and said, our president's still child. I said, he's still alive, but we don't know for how long. And I remember when even the children cried some of them, and none of us could eat. We just couldn't eat our lunch at the right... about 11.30 on the 4th day of the school.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I remember where I was and what I was doing. It's one of those things that sort of gets on your face.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just never forget. Yeah.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I'll help you explain this question, but the question is, what was the most significant thing you've done in your life to support your family? Not necessarily monetary, but what do you think... call it two or three things... Do you think that you've done for your family that neither nobody else could have done or that needed to be done at exactly that time? Well, one thing, there's already an answer to that, which you've told us, is helping your father paying the taxes on the land.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Now, you mean as I was growing up? Is that you, me, or my own son?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Either or both. Okay. Another way to look at that is, what would your family have had to do without if you weren't there? I think you'd have a good guess. I don't know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't know. I mean, I supported my family except to help with the taxes part. I used to buy them medicine clothes, new dress, new clothes, and continue.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I had a cook at my grandmother's for her Christmas.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Plus, when I taught school, I helped with expenses after we were married. Of course, that was years later. We've been married...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: maybe 30 years before I taught school.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I forgot something. We, I mean, after we'd been out here a little while, we ran a dairy. We had a dairy. And we milked 50 cows. And that was before I started. I went back to teaching. And I went back to teaching. We sold the dairy. And I always worked beside her and in the dairy. I never milked, but I carried the milk and put it in the coolers and did the washing and the drying. And then while he was finishing cleaning barns and things, I'd run up and get breakfast. He'd get the kids off to school, and he'd get up. We didn't have breakfast together because we'd get up at 4 in the morning. Ernie did. He did for years.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: 17? I think he had.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: He got up at 4 every morning, but I would try, and I'd get up at 4 as long as I could take it. And no matter how early I went to bed, I just simply couldn't take it too long at 4. I was just too tired. And Ernie would tell me, well, don't do it. Wait until 6 because that was plenty early enough to do the washing. And I would do that a while, and then after a while, I'd think, well, I feel sorry for him down there alone. So I tried again at 4 o'clock, but I couldn't last. So I really was an important member of the dairy family. And our boys were in 4-H. I was a 4-H teacher for years. Both of them went to Chicago as sports winners, and Gary went to Washington, D.C. Four of the outstanding members in the state of Idaho. He was one of the four.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Have you ever entered a county fair or...?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes. I used to take my candy. You used to win a prize? I won first prize in it every year, and I can remember so plainly we had so little during the Depression, and the prize was $7.50. Oh, my, that seemed like so much money.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: That was an awful lot of money. It really was. When did you spend it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, probably in the dresser or something. In the dresser. It didn't go for anything poor.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you keep the books? No. Did you keep the books for the farm?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No. In the days when I was growing up, there were no books kept. There was no income tax. We didn't pay income tax in those days. But since we've had books, and a terrific amount of books, keeping on a farm nowadays, and especially in the partnership my husband and son does, I don't do any of it. Where is much of the books you keep? I don't really give a thing. Because we have our income tax done by an accountant, but they have to get the books ready. What? The internet. Oh, you just can't imagine what keeping is. But after we sold the cows and we didn't even keep the cows in there. So, you know, we wanted to be entirely out of it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you work in the carpentry work of fixing the house and repairing the furniture?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No. Ernie did some, but the buildings he didn't build. But he took all the false seams in and took out the partition. There was a bedroom in that end of the room.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He did a lot of it. And you are responsible for the papering and the decorating?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I do all the paper hanging. He paints. He's a real good painter, but he draws a line that comes paper. He does paper hanging. So I do that all alone. He doesn't even have any idea. I've done all the things I need. I kind of like to do that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How did you learn?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We did it at home. My sister, Maise, and I, we lived in an old house. And we wanted to make it look nice. I would have any paper. You're getting sleepy again.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, I'm not. I'm just smiling. Where did you learn how to refinish the furniture? I just saw. Or did it just come natural?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I probably heard somebody tell me how they did it. I just can't remember exactly how. Somebody probably told us how to do it. We used paint remover. You know how you do it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't know how you do it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A lot of it. Somebody says, what do you do? You use paint remover? Is that all you have to do? They don't know how much sanding we do, do they? No.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I've got a mahogany table. I really didn't want to risk it with the paint remover because I was really afraid my sanding would cost me.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I was like, whoop.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: But I think it was worthwhile. I didn't warp up the grain in the mahogany.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I don't think it ever hurt very much. All of our other things.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: There wasn't any more, but I did it.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And you thought that was the thing to do in those days.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, but I'm never going to do that to it again.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: There's nothing else really exciting that's happened. I almost forgot about the dairy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, we didn't talk about anything the other day. But the dairy here? Mm-hmm.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: The milking barn is where we had our yesteryear. Hm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We're overflowing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: We're overflowing the coffers. And they're overflowing the house.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you sell them or just sell them? No. We're collectors. You're selling them?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: A lot of people have asked what kind of stuff we sell. Well, you would sell one of these, wouldn't you? And I say, no, we're collectors. We don't sell.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I think I already know the answer to this, but I'd like to ask you. If you could go back and make any part of your life over again and could do anything you wanted to do, would you do anything differently? What would change? Would you try anything you haven't done yet?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I can't think of anything too much. The dairy years were hard because we couldn't go anyplace. I think if we could have made a living without the dairy, it would have been much easier. Although it was interesting, we had the registered cows and we kept books on them and studied the bloodlines and knew so many of the other dairymen around and had a real interesting time. But it was what I would call a hard year for the dairy. And we were raising our family then. And we always made good meals and meals on time anyway even though I worked at the barn. Otherwise, I don't think I worked too much. We always loved the farm.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Would you go back to school to get your degree? I'd like you to tell me a little bit more about returning to the university for...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, first summer I went, I took three courses, nine hours. Do you know Dr. Snyder?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Mm-hmm. I know.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Who's retired. Mm-hmm. And his wife taught him.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I have to say, semi-retired. He's still doing a lot of advising.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, you're thinking if it isn't Snyder, I'm sure. Because Dr. Snyder that I'm thinking of, I don't think he is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Is there a... Irvine Snyder? No. Okay. Wrong Snyder.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No. I'm trying to think what his first name is.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And his wife taught him.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Isn't there... I knew him too. Well, anyway, he helped me fill out my form and I had never gone to university. I'd gone to a smaller school. I said, those sound awfully hard.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And he says, they're all hard.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And they were, after not being in school for 40 years or more. They were hard. It wasn't easy.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you like going back?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, I enjoyed it. I especially enjoyed the associations and the lectures. They were interesting, but I didn't like the pay. I remember that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you feel that the students looked down on you? No. Because you were older? No.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I dyed my hair brown, you know, a little bit.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Did you really? Until about two years ago, I did. Oh, it's so pretty down there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, no, I didn't feel like it. Because there were quite a few, especially in some schools. A lot of the teachers go back for a refresher course. So there were lots of older people too. And then I took a lot of correspondence courses too. They were kind of interesting. I didn't mind those too much.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What would be your two or three academic interests? What do you like to study or read about the most?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, the fun part when I was teaching, even though it was the hardest one, going to school, I liked to teach math the best in fourth grade. I enjoyed that. I think I was maybe a better teacher in math than anything I taught. And then I liked science. I grew up on a farm and we always enjoyed the birds and the deer. We had quite a bit of wildlife on our farm. And I always had science there every year in my room.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I keep falling.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Do you want more coffee? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you feel that you influence your husband's thinking? And on what kinds of issues?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I think we do each other. I think we both. I think that I influence his thinking and I think he does mine. But we think more of us. And I feel like we don't have any fights about it. We like that more than anything.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: My husband and I have a couple areas where we just don't get into them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Well, I've seen what he ends in. Our politics are quite similar.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: We go to church together. John is a geologist, of course, not a believer in water riches. I don't believe in water riches. Water riches?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That's the part we disagree a little bit. We don't quarrel about it, but I never could quite understand it. But my husband thinks that there's nothing like it. And we dug a well right here low where you'd think there'd be lots of water, 300 feet, and got enough water to get by for a while when we had to bury. But not nearly enough. We just had a terrible struggle with the water. And finally, we just decided we just couldn't stand it longer. And that was before our kids fell down the hill. Ernie had a water rich town. And of all places to go, careful on the hill. And the alfalfa patch, we found a spot. And we went 200 feet, oh, 10 or 12 feet. And when our family moved up there, of course, they had a town in the shop. They had four bathrooms and washers and dryers like we all have. And we'd go to the well which was good. But they could use all the water they wanted. They watered the lawn, we watered the lawn, watered our garden. So we really think the witching paid off there. I don't know. What do you call those people?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Water witches.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I still, I haven't had that conversation.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I didn't even know what you were talking about. I'm a city girl. Well, people will find water. Yeah, now the kind that go around with the sticks. Do you know the name?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Yes, there's another name. What is that other name they call them? Oh. This man used a stick. And here did he have an iron. Copper.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: He was ironing.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I didn't see him do it. And it was about that. And he said, and he did, he says, now I want you to put the stick here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't want you to put it over here or over here. It's got to be right there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And that driller has to go right where that stick is. And Ernie was there to see that he did. And they did, they got the water. But I'm kind of like you. I can't quite go along with it as strong as he does. I don't quarrel about it. It's fine. We've got wonderful water, and that's important. But I've never quite. And this old man had done a lot of it all around. But he was recently passed away. But he did a great deal of it around this country. He's built many of them. What on earth is that other name they call him? There's another name for him. I can't think of it. But you know, they even write it up in the yearbook that the government puts out about him. And he read in there about him. I have.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I know. Do you like living in a rural area? Have you ever wanted to live in a city?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Never, never wanted to live in a city.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: What do you like about your life here in New York?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I like the privacy we have. Run outside and need underwear if you walk in. I think that's a lot of it.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Don't you get lonely sometimes, though? Or when you were younger, did you feel lonely?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, when I was younger and raising my family, I was busy. But the one thing I never did that you'll think of your lot, I never drove a car.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You never drove a car? And you still don't? How did you get into it?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, I came in with one of the neighbor ladies. Which is too bad. I should have learned here.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I don't know if it does anything.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I have never let myself get lonely. I can always read and waste time. And then I've always had the little organ. And we had a piano. We had a player piano for a recent exhibit. And I've had enough fun with that that I can pass the week. I'm not entertaining anyone else, but I can entertain myself. I can't remember having too much lonely times.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: How do you think that the life that you live

speaker: Speaker 1
words: is different from the life of a woman who lives in a city or the suburbs?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I can sit there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: I feel safer here than I would in a big city. Of course, not having lived that way, it's kind of hard to compare. I wouldn't compare it. I think it would be rather interesting, though, where you go to libraries and come into cities and museums and things like that.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Do you ever take vacations to the cities?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, because the husband doesn't like to drive in the cities.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I don't either.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Dad, I hate to drive around Washington, D.C. Oh, you have, huh?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I lived right outside of here.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Where did you grow up?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I grew up in Michigan. Oh, yes. And you? Upstate New York.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, for goodness sake.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: You think of anything?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: No, I'm not. I'm from Idaho. Yeah, I'm in the area. Well, I fell in love with the West.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I mean, that sounds so hokey and everything else.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: You just came out to go to school or something? Well, I went to school in Bowling Green, Ohio, and I minored in geology. And one way to get a geology minor

speaker: Speaker 2
words: was to go west on what's called a field trip. We got six credits, and we took six weeks,

speaker: Speaker 1
words: and the first part of the summer we toured the west, and then we went to a field camp, an area where we were supposed to navigate. And I just literally fell in love with the West.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I still remember my first mountains. I still remember. I just fell in love with it. I don't want to go back there. I am very excited. I love the Appalachians. They're not chilly mountains. I just love them.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Have you been to southern Idaho much? It's so different, though, isn't it, from northern Idaho? But I don't know southern Idaho. It doesn't seem like a fantasy town. There's various different things, and the mountains are different, and it's all together. Our state is real all about it.
